text: Um a lot of pre amble to have a worn out nugget of "hey are you doing anything fun this weekend". Hard no. That's a) not open ended, and b) can lead into a world of trouble-- funeral, death in the family, privacy issues (sounds a bit nosy for someone you've never met) and really puts people on the defensive. I'd have paid attention to what displays they were going to, and make a related remark: it can be 'that's a new item, and we have additional colours available that are not on display" or compliment them on something they're wearing, sincerely, and quickly, and just leave it at that. I love your pin. She may respond it's an antique, or its an heirloom, or I just picked it up at the thrift store. This is non threatening, and starts a conversation. You can even ask are you here on a mission, that maybe I can help you save time on? (if they seem hurried). Maybe a last minute shower gift, or they just ruined a zipper and badly need a replacement pair of pants. Or maybe they just flew in and don't have anything to wear to a funeral. Help them achieve their goal and send them on their way. You're not building a relationship by wasting their time. If they're browsing and have free time, I've used the "we just got some new pieces in , and if you're not in a hurry, I'd love for you to tell me what you think of them. We love getting feedback. They may even want to try some of these things on, if they're eager to see the latest styles. I've made huge sales doing just this one thing. If they came in your store, they already love what you sell. Now it's a matter of being the expert, and NOT wasting their time. That in itself builds relationships. They now know they can trust you because you won't keep them there for too long.

text: I worked retail for close to 20yrs and had customers follow to wherever I worked next to seek me out because of the service. I have to disagree on the "let me know if you need anything" that you're saying they don't want to hear. Be present as much as possible but also when acknowledging them do say "let me know if you need anything" but also if in a bigger store like I was then let them know when you'll be in a different area so they know where to find you. I developed relationships that were genuine but not with small talk like you're suggesting but real genuine conversations while helping them with their purchases and helping them find the specific product they needed even if it meant taking their number and searching for the best product regardless of if we carried it or not. That also meant when I found that product informing my bosses to start ordering that product because it was the best for the customer's needs. I worked both clothing retail as you're talking about but also home building centers where you really need to know your products and the best for the job they're working on. Biggest thing I can say is be genuine and don't just try to go for the sale at that time but build the relationship so that you have a customer that lasts and will gladly come back and tell others as well. Get your work done other than helping the customer as well but make them see that you're still there and not completely ignored. It's a balance which is rare to see nowadays sadly. I see it more now where you're completely ignored with no one in sight to help when needed rather than greeted and let known that they're willing to help me when I need it. I'm no longer able to work due to severe disabilities and more often than not I'm completely ignored as if they don't want me there and have attitude when I do ask for help. I do understand both sides of retail and don't like asking for help unless absolutely necessary so that makes me want to go somewhere else if they can't offer good customer service.

text: In N.E. Ohio, I've had my cars worked on at one specific auto repair chain that is common to this area. I've had problems with the quality of their work, but I also understand the challenges they face with obtaining and keeping skilled technicians. A couple of years ago I had an oil change and tire rotation and then drove 500 miles to Richmond, VA. Half way through the trip the car began vibrating violently. I pulled over to the side of the interstate, it was very dark and I could not find any problem. I limped the car to the next exit and luckily there was a 24 Hr truck repair facility that agreed to look over my car. The next morning they called me to look at the car and it turned out that the lug nuts were were loose on one of the front wheels. Being an mechanic is hard work and contrary to popular opinion, it takes a lot of brains to be a good mechanic. Add to this that the pay is not very competitive IMO, so what's the incentive for these guys to stay in this profession? I also understand repair costs are a critical factor for the customer, (who also may not be making much money). The franchise in my area also seems to use very cheap parts that do not hold up for more than 3 months. I've stopped using this Auto Repair Chain for brake work because I get feed- back (vibrations) a few months after the brake job is done. I now spend the extra money getting brakes done at the Dealership because they use OEM parts, which the local auto repair chain refuses to use. This problem is a hard nut to crack, I identify with the customers who can barely afford to maintain a car that they are still making high payments on, and I also identify with the mechanics working at these shops who in many cases are doing very difficult work for minimal pay.

Every apprentice in every industry is getting screwed. The boomer generation has a well deserved reputation and one of the main reasons theyre hated is how much gatekeeping they did. It was under their leadership that corporations started requiring college degrees and years of experience to get an entry level job. Unpaid internships were their idea too. And just like in the white collar world, the blue collar world has been gatekept too. 

It used to be, that if you knew how to do a job and could demonstrate that knowledge, you could get licenced and start working and earning decent money RIGHT AWAY. The concept of an apprentice wasnt as wide spread and common. But the boomers, who were eager to eliminate as much competition as possible, started throwing barriers in the way and made working more and more difficult for young people. To the point where now, if you wanna get licensed in a trade, you have to go to school and spend YEARS working under someone who is likely gonna treat you like how a corporation treats an intern. Theyre gonna push all the back breaking grunt work onto you and probably not teach you much because they dont look at it as passing on knowledge to the next generation, they see it as training their future competition

text:
I was at a dealer for a year as a lube tech. I was consistently turning the most hours (not a lot though, not much you can do when oil changes count for .3 LOL) and I got so burned that service advisors started avoiding me for the last hour of the day because I would be in such a sour mood. I started at 16/hr.

After over a year as a lube tech they finally put me in used cars where I did tires and alignments for four months for a dollar more an hour. Had a mentor for a week, after that I was on my own. Whenever I asked about apprenticeship or testing for ASEs my boss laughed me off.

I’ve been in an independent shop for a few months now. I’m doing timing chains for 16/hr. My new boss complained about me stealing his tools all the time, and then got mad when I told him he doesn’t pay me enough to go on the tool truck and buy specialty stuff. I’m barely able to keep my car in working order, can’t afford to move out of my parent’s place, and never have the energy to do anything on the weekends. I’ve let my boss know about these struggles and he pulled the classic small business owner move, “we don’t have it easy either.” While he drove to work in one of his four vehicles from his newly built 300k home.

By all means, my sob story is nowhere near the worst. I recognized the dealer trap pretty early, and my new shop is generally a low stress environment besides the low pay. I just finally got a $1 bump. But I don’t foresee myself in this industry much longer. All my friends from highschool and the dealer have moved into other industries and not only are they making more, but they have more free time and more energy to enjoy that free time. I don’t understand how an industry can sustain itself when it chews and spits people out like automotive does. It’s honestly a miracle it hasn’t completely collapsed already.

text: Probably the easiest and most straightforward conversion would be to buy a salvage model three performance(so you have all-wheel-drive, 500hp , 🔋 72kwhr, plus software track mode to disable traction control if you need to off road ) . After that, weld the body of your truck on that skateboard. you have all the hardest parts taken care of. Like using Tesla’s bms using Tesla software ,using Tesla regen software programs, plus all the app connectivity like cameras, opening your door and summoning the car from your phone. Also, because the first generation model three has a Steel unibody and a regular old steel subframe you can easily fabricate long travel suspension for truck off road. it’s not aluminum giga cast like the cyber truck or model y . basically the hardest part will be metal fabrication and bodywork. Not worrying about high-voltage lines, battery management and many many other critical software control things that electric vehicles need plus all the mechanical stuff like braking ,steering and all the things you mentioned that make a big difference in electric vehicle efficiency. Get the skateboard , weld the body on with a matching wheel base , that’s the best.
